bull_bear.body:
- Debt free: the Company prepaid in December 2022 the financial assistance obtained in earlier years and, as at the Balance Sheet date, does not have any Secured Borrowing; MD&A states it 'is now debt free for past 2-3 years'.
- Improved cash collection discipline from state utilities via the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' online portal, which the Company says forces State Electricity Companies to settle dues on due date and has facilitated regular cash flow.
- Active portfolio pruning: the Company closed down loss-making and low-tariff wind farms in Andhra Pradesh and a unit in Tamil Nadu, and retired wind mills that had outlived their technical life.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Total dependence on renewable-energy policy of Centre and State Governments and on State Electricity Regulatory Commissions — MD&A states 'The performance of the Company is directly linked to the Renewable Energy Policies of both Centre and State Governments, effectiveness of Nodal Agencies and formulation of encouraging policies and implementation thereof by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions.' The Company has no control over the single variable that sets its revenue.
- Unremunerative and inflation-frozen tariffs — MD&A says in many states tariffs 'have not being encouraging' and that tariff remains fixed for many years with no adjustment to inflation or the factual cost of repairs and establishment costs, so ageing wind mills 'may prove uneconomical' even with good operation and maintenance.
- Open-access charges blocking third-party sales — MD&A: 'sale to third parties are being discouraged by imposing high open access charges under one pretext or other', which the Company reads as continued regulatory support for conventional energy and which closes off the higher-realisation merchant channel.
- Receivable delays from state utilities against a fixed cost base — MD&A: 'In the wind power business the expenses are more or less fixed, the delayed receipt of generation proceeds necessitate that company has to resort to temporary borrowings to tide over the mismatch. This is also a concern as it has to bear the brunt of finance cost.' Partially mitigated by the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' portal, which has helped the Company tackle liquidity issues.
- Inordinate delays in adjudication by regulators, APTEL and High Courts — MD&A: 'inordinate delays in adjudication of the matters by Electricity Regulatory Commission, Appellate Tribunal for Electricity and even High courts result in acute pressure on the Company due to huge mismatch in inflow and outflow of funds', and the same delays are 'impeding the future projects'.
- Sub-scale position in a sector that has consolidated toward large players — MD&A repeatedly states that 'present environment in Green Energy is only for Big Players with deep pockets developing in terms of thousands of MW', that such houses can absorb running losses and negotiate better with utilities due to their size, and that many small and medium entities that entered two decades back have closed their units. Karma operates about 30.50 MW.
- Ageing asset base driving volatile operation, maintenance and repair costs — MD&A's ratio commentary attributes the year's loss and the adverse interest coverage and net profit margin to 'higher Operation and Maintenance Costs, repairs to Wind mills at different sites' despite improved turnover; wind mills that outlived their technical life have had to be retired and units in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu were closed.
- Listing-compliance and regulatory-penalty exposure — The Corporate Governance Report discloses a SEBI adjudication and settlement process over deviations from the Listing Regulations, with an order issued on 10th July 2025 imposing a penalty which the Company remitted, and BSE notices received on 6th April 2026 for non-compliance with Regulation 17(1) of SEBI LODR for the quarters ended 30th September 2024 and 31st December 2024, with penalties since paid.

outlook.body: The annual report discloses no expansion or new capex project. The direction is the opposite: the MD&A states the Company now has about 30.50 MW of power generating wind farms and had closed down loss-making and low-tariff wind farms in Andhra Pradesh and a unit in Tamil Nadu, and that wind mills which have outlived their technical life — where continued operation even with good operation and maintenance may prove uneconomical because tariffs remain fixed with no adjustment for inflation or actual repair and establishment costs — have been retired. Management observes that the huge outlay needed to meet Central Government renewable targets means only big business houses with deep pockets are entering the Green Power space, and that delays by state utilities, State Electricity Regulatory Commissions and higher judicial authorities are impeding future projects. Existing wind farms are located at Theni and Tirunelveli in Tamil Nadu and Beed and Satara in Maharashtra. The Board's report confirms there was no change in the business of the company during the year and that no new business was commenced or products introduced in FY 2025-26.

outlook.body:
- Company performance is directly linked to the Renewable Energy Policies of both Centre and State Governments, the effectiveness of Nodal Agencies, and the formulation and implementation of encouraging policies by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions.
- Wind power 'has lost its bite': in many states tariffs have not been encouraging and sale to third parties is discouraged through high open access charges, with continued regulatory support for conventional energy.
- The Green Energy environment now favours only big players with deep pockets developing in thousands of MW, who can absorb running losses and negotiate better with utilities; many small and medium entities that entered two decades back have closed their units.
- In the wind power business expenses are more or less fixed, so delayed receipt of generation proceeds forces temporary borrowings and finance cost — mitigated recently by the Prapti portal.
- FY2025-26 margins were hurt by higher Operation and Maintenance costs and repairs to wind mills at different sites despite improved turnover.
- Macro backdrop cited: Indian economy resilient in 2025-26 with real GDP estimated to grow 7.6 per cent and real GVA growth of 7.7 per cent; real GDP growth for 2026-27 projected at 6.9 per cent; Government focus on scaling up domestic manufacturing and GST rationalisation in Union Budget 2026-27.
- Tariffs remain fixed for many years with no adjustment for inflation or the actual cost of repairs and establishment costs, pressuring economics of ageing turbines.

Management observes that the huge outlay needed to meet Central Government renewable targets means only big business houses with deep pockets are entering the Green Power space, and that delays by state utilities, State Electricity Regulatory Commissions and higher judicial authorities are impeding future projects. Existing wind farms are located at Theni and Tirunelveli in Tamil Nadu and Beed and Satara in Maharashtra. The Board's report confirms there was no change in the business of the company during the year and that no new business was commenced or products introduced in FY 2025-26.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Debt free: the Company prepaid in December 2022 the financial assistance obtained in earlier years and, as at the Balance Sheet date, does not have any Secured Borrowing; MD&A states it 'is now debt free for past 2-3 years'.
- Improved cash collection discipline from state utilities via the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' online portal, which the Company says forces State Electricity Companies to settle dues on due date and has facilitated regular cash flow.
- Active portfolio pruning: the Company closed down loss-making and low-tariff wind farms in Andhra Pradesh and a unit in Tamil Nadu, and retired wind mills that had outlived their technical life.

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Total dependence on renewable-energy policy of Centre and State Governments and on State Electricity Regulatory Commissions — MD&A states 'The performance of the Company is directly linked to the Renewable Energy Policies of both Centre and State Governments, effectiveness of Nodal Agencies and formulation of encouraging policies and implementation thereof by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions.' The Company has no control over the single variable that sets its revenue.
- Unremunerative and inflation-frozen tariffs — MD&A says in many states tariffs 'have not being encouraging' and that tariff remains fixed for many years with no adjustment to inflation or the factual cost of repairs and establishment costs, so ageing wind mills 'may prove uneconomical' even with good operation and maintenance.
- Open-access charges blocking third-party sales — MD&A: 'sale to third parties are being discouraged by imposing high open access charges under one pretext or other', which the Company reads as continued regulatory support for conventional energy and which closes off the higher-realisation merchant channel.
- Receivable delays from state utilities against a fixed cost base — MD&A: 'In the wind power business the expenses are more or less fixed, the delayed receipt of generation proceeds necessitate that company has to resort to temporary borrowings to tide over the mismatch. This is also a concern as it has to bear the brunt of finance cost.' Partially mitigated by the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' portal, which has helped the Company tackle liquidity issues.
- Inordinate delays in adjudication by regulators, APTEL and High Courts — MD&A: 'inordinate delays in adjudication of the matters by Electricity Regulatory Commission, Appellate Tribunal for Electricity and even High courts result in acute pressure on the Company due to huge mismatch in inflow and outflow of funds', and the same delays are 'impeding the future projects'.
- Sub-scale position in a sector that has consolidated toward large players — MD&A repeatedly states that 'present environment in Green Energy is only for Big Players with deep pockets developing in terms of thousands of MW', that such houses can absorb running losses and negotiate better with utilities due to their size, and that many small and medium entities that entered two decades back have closed their units. Karma operates about 30.50 MW.
- Ageing asset base driving volatile operation, maintenance and repair costs — MD&A's ratio commentary attributes the year's loss and the adverse interest coverage and net profit margin to 'higher Operation and Maintenance Costs, repairs to Wind mills at different sites' despite improved turnover; wind mills that outlived their technical life have had to be retired and units in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu were closed.
- Listing-compliance and regulatory-penalty exposure — The Corporate Governance Report discloses a SEBI adjudication and settlement process over deviations from the Listing Regulations, with an order issued on 10th July 2025 imposing a penalty which the Company remitted, and BSE notices received on 6th April 2026 for non-compliance with Regulation 17(1) of SEBI LODR for the quarters ended 30th September 2024 and 31st December 2024, with penalties since paid.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Cost reduction, tight cash flow management and pursuit of policy changes to mitigate the sector downturn.
- Rationalise the fleet: close loss-making and low-tariff wind farms (Andhra Pradesh, one unit in Tamil Nadu) and retire wind mills that have outlived their technical life where continued operation is uneconomical.
- Stay debt free by using improved realisation of generation dues from state utilities, having pre-paid the bank term loans.
- Use the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' online portal, registering invoice details so State Electricity Companies settle dues on due date, to keep cash flow …

hero.oneLiner: Karma Energy Limited is a small Indian renewable-power generator operating about 30.50 MW of wind farms and selling wind power to state utilities and third parties.
